extraction.name: MATH
extraction.description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems. Each problem features a full step-by-step solution which can be used to teach models to generate answer derivations and explanations.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks (UC Berkeley); Collin Bums (UC Berkeley); Saurav Kadavath (UC Berkeley); Akul Arora (UC Berkeley); Steven Basart (UChicago); Eric Tang (UC Berkeley); Dawn Song (UC Berkeley); Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley)
extraction.citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt. Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021).
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The MATH dataset was collected by sourcing problems from mathematics competitions (such as AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME) from the Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) website. The AMPS pretraining dataset was assembled by pulling problems from Khan Academy and generating problems using manually designed Mathematica scripts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: High school mathematics competition problems from aops.com, Khan Academy exercises, and problems generated via Mathematica computer algebra system scripts.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Solving the MATH dataset with machine learning would be of profound practical and intellectual significance, though attaining high accuracy could have ramifications for cheating on homework.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: To measure the problem-solving ability of machine learning models; to better forecast reasoning capabilities.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: During pretraining, we upsample Khan Academy data by a factor of 5 and we downsample Mathematica by a factor of 2 to account for the large difference in dataset sizes.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To assess models using exact match, we force the final boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules. Specifically, probabilities are expressed as simplified fractions. Moreover, matrix entry fractions are encoded with x/y, while all other fractions are consistently encoded with the \frac{x}{y} command. Coefficients are encoded without a multiplication symbol (e.g. 5xnot5*x). Expressions with multiple variables are entered in alphabetical order; polynomials are expressed in decreasing degree order.
